title: No-Call/No-Show: How to Cover the Shift and Prevent the Next One
summary: Learn what a no-call/no-show is, what to do in the first hour, and how to set up call-outs, schedules, and coverage so fewer shifts go empty.
body_markdown:
The 6 a.m. opener hasn’t walked in, hasn’t called, and isn’t answering texts. The manager has a line forming and about 20 minutes to find cover. That gap is a no-call/no-show, and the missed hours are the smallest part of the bill. A coworker works overtime to fill the shift, service slips on a short floor, and the manager loses the morning to phone calls.


Most of what happens next is operational. The fastest recoveries come from teams that already know who to call, who can cover, and how a worker is supposed to say they can’t make it, and the same setup keeps the next slot from going empty.


## What is a no-call/no-show?


A


[no-call/no-show](https://intranet.uchicago.edu/policies/human-resources-policies/500-599-time-off/502-attendance-absenteeism-tardiness-and-job-abandonment) (NCNS) is a scheduled shift the worker misses without notifying the designated contact through an approved channel by the notice deadline.


Four situations look identical on a schedule grid and need different handling:


1. **Timely call-out:** The worker misses the shift but gives notice by the required method and deadline. The shift still needs cover, but it isn’t an NCNS.


2. **Lateness:** The worker arrives late. Your attendance policy sets the point where late becomes absent, so check it before logging the shift.


3. **Approved swap:** Two coworkers documented a trade, so the shift belongs to the coworker who took it.


4. **Scheduling error:** The worker wasn’t on the posted schedule or saw an outdated version. Fix the schedule record so the miss isn’t logged against them.


Check the posted schedule, notice log, and swap record before calling an empty slot an NCNS.


## What does a no-call/no-show cost?


The


[direct costs of an absence](https://www.shrm.org/content/dam/en/shrm/topics-tools/news/employee-relations/Total-Financial-Impact-of-Employee-Absences-Report.pdf) include overtime, replacement workers, and the output coworkers lose when they fill in. The indirect costs arrive later, when the reliable people who keep covering the same slot wear down and start looking elsewhere. None of that shows up on the overtime line.


A per-incident number beats any national average. Pull one recent coverage record and fill in your own figures:


**Incident cost = (hours covered by overtime × base wage × your overtime multiplier) + (hours covered by agency or temp labor × agency rate) + (manager hours spent finding cover × manager hourly rate) + (lost sales or output during hours nobody covered)**


For illustration, an 8-hour shift at a $16 base wage, covered at 1.5x overtime, costs $192. Add one hour of a $28-per-hour manager’s time, and the incident reaches $220 before lost sales.


## What should you do when an employee doesn’t show up?


Welfare and coverage come first, and documentation runs alongside both:


1. **Reach the worker:** Call the mobile number, then any secondary number, then text: “We expected you at \[time\] today and have not heard from you. Please contact me as soon as possible.”


2. **Call the emergency contact when there’s a real welfare concern:** One public-sector


[no-call/no-show process](https://des.wa.gov/services/small-agency-support/human-resources/employee-toolkit/no-call-no-show-process) moves to emergency contacts when the worker hasn’t responded within one hour. That information is a


[confidential personnel record](https://kb.wisc.edu/smphhr/127610) , and a welfare check belongs to emergency services.


3. **Start coverage in parallel:** Offer the open shift to qualified workers while outreach continues, not after it.


4. **Document everything:** Log every attempt with a time stamp, who covered, the incident cost, and the worker’s account on return.


Coverage is where most of the hour goes. Anything beyond the shift itself, including attendance records, discipline, or questions about protected leave, belongs with your HR team and employment counsel, so hand them the log and let them take it from there.

- **One channel:** Pick one way to call out, such as a call-in line or the scheduling app, and use it at every location. When one supervisor accepts texts and another accepts social media messages, workers stop knowing which one counts.


- **A named contact for every shift:** Name the manager on duty or a role, not “whoever’s around.”


- **A clear cutoff:** Set a time such as 30 minutes before the shift, so the manager still has room to find cover.


- **A confirmation reply:** Send a short acknowledgment so the worker knows the message landed.


- **A swap path:** Give workers a way to offer the shift to a coworker before calling out, so the gap can close without the manager.


Explain all five in writing during onboarding and repeat them in the first-week schedule message, since a worker who has never been told the cutoff can’t meet it. Two short messages cover most of the communication:


Shift reminder (sent the day before): Hi \[name\], you’re on tomorrow at \[location\] from \[start\] to \[end\], reporting to \[manager\]. Can’t make it? Reply here or swap in the app at least 30 minutes before your shift.


Call-out confirmation: Thanks for letting us know, \[name\]. Your \[date\] shift is being covered. Reply here if anything changes.


Keep both messages short, in the worker’s preferred language, and sent from the same channel every time.


## How to reduce no-shows before they happen


Prevention starts with predictable schedules and support for workers’ real barriers. In


[retail timecard data](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/drivers_late_abs_8e537441-25da-4dd4-9434-9f285a6584eb.pdf) , a changed workday or a start time moved by more than an hour was linked to more lateness and absence. Caregiving shows up too, with


[child care problems](https://www2.census.gov/library/working-papers/2026/demo/sehsd-wp2026-08.pdf) costing affected households weeks of work time.


The fixes line up against those causes:


- **Finish preboarding before Day 1:** Close out paperwork, uniform, start time, and who to report to, and confirm the


[first-shift details](https://www.fountain.com/posts/best-practices-for-successful-employee-onboarding) in writing.


- **Publish schedules predictably:** A


[consistent posted schedule](https://www.fountain.com/workforce-management-guide) is the main lever, and a reminder is a courtesy on top of it.


- **Plan around caregiving and commute barriers:** When a worker’s start times keep colliding with child care or transit, a steadier shift pattern does more than another reminder, and the


[day-to-day pressures](https://www.fountain.com/posts/challenges-faced-by-frontline-workers) frontline workers face are worth asking about at hire.


- **Offer a mobile way to swap:** A swap completed in one of the


[scheduling apps](https://www.fountain.com/posts/ai-shift-scheduling-tools) before the shift is a gap that never opens.


- **Keep a qualified coverage roster on standby:** Cross-trained workers who’ve opted into open-shift alerts turn an hour of calls into one broadcast.


Track three numbers: no-show rate by site and manager, Day 1 no-shows against tenured no-shows, and time to fill the gap. A cluster at one site points to that site’s scheduling and leadership first.


At


[Stitch Fix](https://www.fountain.com/customer/stitch-fix) fulfillment centers, the share of “applicants who pass background checks and show up on day one” rose from 68% to 95% after hiring was automated.

## Frequently asked questions about no-call/no-shows


### What should a manager do first when an employee doesn’t show up?


Check on the worker and start coverage at the same time. Call, then text, and contact the emergency contact only if there’s a genuine welfare concern, while the open shift goes out to qualified coworkers. Log each attempt as you go.


### What’s the difference between a no-call/no-show and a call-out?


A call-out is a missed shift with notice through the approved channel before the cutoff. A no-call/no-show is a missed shift with no notice at all. A call-out leaves time to find cover, while a no-call/no-show usually surfaces at the start time.


### How do you reduce Day 1 no-shows?


Finish paperwork before the first shift, confirm the start time, location, uniform, and contact in writing, and answer new-hire questions quickly. Day 1 no-shows can start with silence between offer acceptance and the first shift, so close that gap first.
